claims.text: Aging HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C induces nanoscale precipitates or local segregation zones.
Rapid cooling after aging at 600–800 °C preserves more residual internal stress than slow cooling.
The residual internal stresses arise from differential thermal contraction between the matrix and precipitates or segregation-driven regions.
Slow cooling permits partial relaxation of thermal-mismatch-induced stresses.
Residual stresses pre-stress and modify the dislocation network.
Residual stresses lower the effective activation barrier for dislocation slip.
Residual stresses lower the effective activation barrier for dislocation climb.
Lower barriers for slip and climb lead to enhanced high-temperature tensile creep rates.
Rapidly quenched samples will have higher tensile creep rates at 1250 °C than slow-cooled samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will exhibit higher residual-stress levels than slow-cooled samples.
Preserved residual stresses will alter elastic-modulus trends over 293–1100 K relative to slow-cooled samples.
Rapidly quenched and slow-cooled samples will show distinct post-aging hardening behavior.
Residual-stress effects provide a unified explanation for creep acceleration, temperature-dependent elastic moduli, and post-aging hardening.
X-ray diffraction or an equivalent technique can be used to measure residual-stress profiles for correlation with mechanical responses.
The proposed effects are expected to be most pronounced within the stated aging window of 600–800 °C and testing range of 293 K to 1250 °C.
